trigonal prisms, while the latter are formed when three Ln2 polyhedra in each layer are linked through the O4/F site to form 60º rotated Ln(2)3O19 units. The Ln polyhedra are linked via edge-sharing of the Ln1 with three Ln2 columns. The isolated SiO tetrahedra are located between the lanthanide columns and have freedom to tilt [59]. Pressure causes its tilting and changes in the configuration of the channels and related physical properties [59]. More information may be found in the work of Zhang et al. [59] whose main objective was to study the pressure-induced structural transformation of the rare earth non-stoichiometric silicates RE9.33(SiO4)6O2 by crystallography, photoluminescence, infrared spectroscopy and DFT calculations. The photoluminescent studies on the europium-containing compounds prepared by Latshaw et al. [61] demonstrated that the excitation (emission at 607 nm) and emission (excitation at 230 nm) data are almost identical, suggesting that modifying the ratio of the cation atoms on the Ln sites and of the anion atoms does not change the luminescence. No important features were observed for the gadolinium-containing compound.

Recently, Heyward and co-workers [60] studied the solid-state chemistry of novel metal silicate apatite crystals containing Eu2+ and Eu3+ prepared with hightemperature hydrothermal fluids (Eu10(SiO4)6O2 and NaEu9(SiO4)6O2). The room temperature photoluminescence studies were used to evaluate the europium oxidation state and optical behaviour. In fact, the excitation at 370 nm was used to probe the blue (\~435 nm) emission characteristic of Eu2+ in Eu (SiO ) O , as well as the red (\~615 nm) emission characteristic of Eu3+ in NaEu9(SiO4)6O2. Thus, the authors concluded that Eu10(SiO4)6O2 possesses the formal charges EuII2EuIII8(SiO4)6O2, where Eu2+ is responsible for structural charge balancing. Since no traces of Eu2+ were found in NaEu9(SiO4)6O2, charge balancing is exclusively done by Na+.
## Other materials

The microporous zirconosilicate with formula Na5Zr2Si6O18(Cl,OH)·2H2O (known as AV-3, analogue of petarasite, a rare mineral found in Mont St. Hilaire, Quebéc, Canada) was synthesized by Lin and co-workers [35] and is a system suitable for lanthanide incorporation. The incorporation of RE metals in the structure was made by adding MCl3 (M = Y and Eu) into precursor of the hydrothermal synthesis, resulting in novel lanthanide zirconosilicates containing stoichiometric amounts of M3+ cations (with a Zr/M ratio of 4). Figure 15 shows the framework of AV-3, built up of corner-sharing SiO4 tetrahedra linked by ZrO6 octahedra, forming 6-membered ring elliptical channels, running down the b- and c-axis [103]. There are also 6-membered ring channels running parallel to the a- and c-axis. Metal ions may be incorporated into AV-3 by replacing Zr4+ or/and Na+. If only sodium cations are replaced, the Si/Zr ratio will be ca. 3 and the Cl- content will increase. If the metals only replaces Zr4+, the chloride anion content should decrease. Previous research on AV-3 materials revealed that it collapses when Cl- and OH- are removed. In fact, the incorporation of europium and yttrium in the AV-3 framework clearly expands the unit cell in all three directions, increases its volume significantly and at the same time reduces the chloride anion content. Lin et al., [35] also indicated that the photoluminescence spectroscopy (see Figure 16) suggests that Eu3+ only occupies one main site (see Table 1) and postulated that Eu predominantly occupy Zr positions. In fact, the number of Stark components observed for the 5D05F1 and 5D07F2 transitions (3 and 5, respectively) indicates that the Eu3+ ions occupy a site of low symmetry without an inversion centre (considering the relative intensity of the 5D05F2 and 5D05F1 lines). Moreover, no significant difference was observed for the 5D05F0–4 transitions excited at different wavelengths, which suggests that Eu3+ ions occupy a single site. The spectrum also exhibits a broad and faint band in the range 380–570 nm, attributed to electron–hole recombination mechanisms occurring within the AV-3 host [28].

The microporous lanthanides AV-24, whose general formula is K7[Ln3Si12O32]·xH2O (Ln = Sm3+, Eu3+, Gd3+, Tb3+) and belong to the family of phyllosilicates, were synthesized by Ananias and co-workers [50]. The authors describe it as a material possessing phenomenal photoluminescent properties since it is the first example of an extended solid in which Ln3+-Ln3+ dimers (inter-Ln distance ca. 3.9 Å) are embedded in the framework and behave like a molecule. Previous studies had been made by Pushcharovskii and co-workers [51] and by Haile et al., [52,53] on this family of materials. The former described the K8-x[Yb3Si12O32](OH)1-x·xH2O with x ca. 2/3 while the latter studied the fast ion conductivity of rare-earth silicates with a very similar structure. As can be seen in Figure 17, the structure of these AV-24 materials is built up of six crystallographic distinct SiO4 that polymerize in the bc plane into anionic [Si12O32]n16n- layers, exhibiting a periodic alternation between two types of 6-, one type of 8-, and a highly distorted 12-membered rings. Those layers pile up in a parallel fashion along the [100] direction, leading to the formation of 8-membered ring tunnels with an effective cross section of ca. 3.2 Å × 3.2 Å where potassium cations and water molecules are accommodated with high disorder. Adjacent layers are connected by two crystallographic distinct lanthanide centres, Ln1 and Ln2, both coordinated by six SiO4 tetrahedra. Ln1 is located at a crystallographic inversion centre while Ln2 appears as centrosymmetric binuclear units. The photoluminescent studies made on Eu-AV-24 (see Figure 18) were in good agreement with the published X-ray diffraction data. The ligand field splits of the 5D07F1 and 5D07F2 transitions into more than three and five Stark components, respectively, indicated the presence of two distinct Eu3+ environments (see Table 1). The results also explained that the embedded Eu3+-Eu3+ dimers behave like a molecule since the emission is unique and have the longest 5D0 lifetime (detection at 589.6 nm) so far observed for Eu3+ in solids (10.29 ± 0.04 ms at 12 K). Based on these studies, the authors discovered that these dimers are energetically more stable than the individual metal ions, because the energy of transition is lower than the corresponding energy of each individual constituent Eu3+ ion. In addition, a complex and an unusual energy transfer dynamics between the distinct Eu3+ ions presented were assisted. A nonradiative energy transfer from the isolated Eu1 ions to the Eu2-Eu2 dimers occurs at 12 K while at temperatures above 50 K a second, thermally activated, energy transfer process occurs from the dimers to the isolated Eu1 ions [50].

In 2010, a family of microporous lanthanide silicates, K Ln Si O NO ·H O (Ln = Sm3+, Eu3+, Gd3+, Tb3+) was synthesized under mild hydrothermal conditions at 503 K by Wang and co-workers [54] for ion exchange applications. The single-crystal structural analysis revealed that each asymmetric unit contains twelve crystallographically distinct Si atoms, three distinct Ln atoms (see Table 1), one distinct N atom, and nine distinct K atoms. All Ln atoms are six-coordinated to O atoms. The SiO4 tetrahedra and the LnO6 octahedra are connected by sharing vertex O atoms to form a three dimensional framework which contains 8-membered ring channels along the [100] direction. Potassium cations and NO - anions reside in the free void space to balance the framework charge. The structure can be viewed as constructed from [Si3O8]n4n- layers linked by LnO6 octahedra. In each layer, the SiO4 tetrahedra share oxygen atoms with others to form two types of 6-, an 8- and a 12-membered rings along [001] direction. The nearby layers are linked by LnO6 octahedra to form 3D framework. The Ln(1)O octahedron connects with six SiO tetrahedra while the dimer formed by Ln(2)O6 and Ln(3)O6 octahedra links to ten SiO4 tetrahedra of the silicate layer. K+ and NO3- ions are orderly arranged in the void space of the 3D framework. Furthermore, K1-K4 and K6-K7 cations are slightly away from 8-membered ring channels, while K5 cations lie within the 6-rings of the [Si3O8]n4n-. K8 and K9 cations and the NO3- anions are centrally located within the 8-membered ring channels.

The structure of this material is closely related to those Ln-silicates described previously, K8-x[Yb3Si12O32](OH)1-x·xH2O [65], K8[Nd3Si12O32](OH) [52,53] and [K9F2][Ln3Si12O32] with Ln = Sm3+, Eu3+, Gd3+ [26]. The basic differences are the lanthanide species and locations of the anions. In the latter, the fluoride atoms are tightly bonded to K atoms to form K2F7 units, which are centred at the 8-membered ring channels and therefore the F- anions are not dissociative. In the material synthesized by Wang et al., [54], the large amount of K+ and the fact that the NO3- anions are centrally located in the 8-membered ring channels enabled the ion movement, which means this Ln-silicate may exhibit ion exchange capacity. Preliminary ion exchange experiments indicated that part of NO3- ion groups could be exchanged with halides (F-> Cl- > Br-) without loss of crystallinity. The principal result of the photoluminescence studies on this material suggested the presence of three Ln3+ environments, in agreement with single-crystal X-ray results. In particular, the room temperature decay curve detected for the 5D07F2 (611 nm) transition of EuSiO-CJ3 (excitation at 266 nm) can be well fitted by a tri-exponential function, yielding the lifetimes of 2.06, 3.12 and 0.47 ms [54]. The lifetimes of 0.27, 1.88 and 3.99 ms were found after fitting the room temperature decay curve detected at the 5D47F5 (542 nm) transition of TbSiO-CJ3 (excitation at 266 nm).

Only a few number of papers dealing with lanthanide fluoride-containing materials have been published. For instance, with europium, compounds like KEu IIFSi O [57], Eu2IIEu3IIIF(SiO4)3 [58] and K2EuSi4O10F [41] were documented. It is worth mentioning that the latter is the first synthetic fluoride-silicate that comprises a 3D framework containing 6- and 8-membered rings channels that are delimited by tubular SiO chains and 1D chains of EuO4F2 octahedra along the [010] direction. Chiang et al., [25] reported the synthesis, the crystal structure and the luminescence properties of a new europium fluoride silicate, K5Eu2FSi4O13. The preparation of Ln-silicates using a fluoride flux is of interest since the method prevents the presence of hydroxyl groups and water molecules that are often detrimental to photoluminescence properties due to quenching effects [25]. Furthermore, the introduction of a second type of anion may possibly potentiate the optical properties of lanthanide silicates. A substantial number of new microporous mixed-framework silicates containing octahedrally coordinated metal(III) cations (V3+, Cr3+, Fe3+, In3+ and rare-earth elements) were prepared via the fluxmethod by the group of Tillmanns in Viena, Austria. Although, no photoluminescence properties were reported, several systems deserve consideration, such as K2.9Rb0.1[ErSi3O9] [62], Ba[RE2Si3O10] (RE3+ = Gd3+, Er3+, Yb3+, Sc3+) and Sr[Y2Si3O10] [63], BaK[YSi2O7] and Cs3[YSi8O19] [64], (Rb,Cs)9[Y7Si24O63] [27].

The structure synthesized by Chiang et al., [25] is constructed by an unbranched tetrasilicate Si4O13 tetramer, a dimer of vertex-sharing octahedra Eu2FO10, and five potassium sites. The octahedral dimer consists of two octahedra with a fluorine atom as common vertex and connects to ten SiO4 tetrahedra, which belong to six different silicate tetramers. Each tetramer connects to six dimers forming a 3D framework with 5- and 6-membered ring channels along the b-axis. K1 is located in a cage surrounded by two dimers and six tetrahedra, K2 and K3 are in cages surrounded by two dimers

and two 6-membered rings formed by two octahedra and four tetrahedra. K4 and K5 are in cages surrounded by three 6-membered rings formed by two octahedra and four tetrahedra and three 4-membered rings formed by two octahedra and two tetrahedra. Figure 19 illustrates a photoluminescence study of this material. The existence of two Eu3+ local environments (see Table 1) is clearly indicated by the presence of two peaks attributed to the 5D07F0 transition. Curiously, the two emission lines corresponding to the 5D07F0 transition had the same decay curves either they were excited at 532 nm or 473 nm, which indicated no difference in the 5D0 state radiative lifetimes of the two Eu3+ sites (2.0 ± 01 ms). These decay curves indicated that the observed emission was a simple radiative process (no other nonradiative processes occurred in the 5D state), and pointed out that these two Eu3+ local environments are quite similar. Both observations were in accordance with crystallographic data.

Wierzbicka-Wieczorek et al. [67,104] reported the synthesis and the structural and optical properties of several new silicates crystallized from high-temperature flux mixtures. Deserves highlight the series of measurements of the structural and photoluminescent properties of mixed-framework rare earth barium yttrium sorosilicates [104] The work indicated that Ln3+ cations substitute octahedrally coordinated Y3+ sites in different proportions but roughly in correspondence to the Y:Ln ratio in the flux mixtures. Increasing the amount of substitution decreases the photoluminescence emission intensity (concentration self-quenching).

Latshaw and co-workers [69] just published the low-temperature preparation of Na ScSiO (OH) and Na YbSiO (OH) crystals using a sodium hydroxide based hydroflux along with the high-temperature preparation of crystals of NaLaSiO4 and NaYbSiO using a sodium fluoride/sodium chloride eutectic flux. Na ScSiO (OH) and Na2YbSiO4(OH) possess two unique Si sites, two unique RE sites, four Na sites and ten oxygen sites. Both Si environments result in isolated SiO4 units that are cornershared to two RE(1)O and to two RE(2)O octahedra. On the other hand, both RE sites corner-share to two Si(1)O4 and to two Si(2)O4, plus to two of the other RE octahedra. The hydroxyl groups are presumably located at the O(9) and O(10) sites, which make up the corner-shared sites of the RE octahedra. The four Na sites are placed in the channels. The NaYbSiO4 structure contains one unique Na, one unique Si, one unique Yb, and three unique O sites, while the NaLaSiO4 structure contains three unique La, three unique Si, three unique Na, and twelve unique O sites. The Yb atoms of the former are located in a distorted YbO octahedra that corner-shares with other YbO octahedra and corner- and edge-share to SiO tetrahedra. The three La sites of the latter are eight-coordinated and all are edge- and corner-shared to isolated SiO units and corner- and face-shared with other La polyhedra. The SiO tetrahedra of

NaYbSiO are isolated from each other and contribute to the overall structure only via corner- and edge-sharing with YbO octahedra, which transforms the 2D sheets of the Yb polyhedra to a 3D structure. The sodium atoms fill the channels between the Yb and Si polyhedra. The Si atoms of NaLaSiO4 form isolated SiO4 units and the Na atoms are positioned in the channels along a-axis. No photoluminescent studies were presented.

A lot of research has been focused on the synthesis of metal silicate under hightemperature and high-pressure conditions, however this is not a new field of research. For example, the previously referred HCs3Ti4O4(SiO4)3·4H2O, analogue ivanyukite, was prepared at 750º C and ca. 30 000 psi by Harrison et al. [105]. Furthermore, Lii and his research group carried out an extensive work on this field by synthesizing a series of metal silicates including niobium silicates [106], vanadium silicates [107], indium silicates [108], stannosilicates [109] and uranium silicates [110–112]. Haile and coworkers [113,114] were the first reporting the successful synthesis of neodymium and yttrium silicates at high temperatures and pressures, seeking for fast alkali ion conductors. Moreover, Huang et al., [24] published a new europium silicate Cs3EuSi6O15 synthesized at 600 ºC and 170 MPa, and investigated its crystal structure and luminescence properties. The structure consists of loop-branched vierer double chains of silicate with four-, six- (where the six-coordinated europium atoms are located between them) and 8-membered rings, which are connected via 10-membered rings at their interfaces to form a 3D silicate framework. More recently, Liu et al. reported the high-temperature and high-pressure hydrothermal synthesis, crystal structure and photoluminescent properties of Na15Eu3Si12O36 [41], K2EuSi4O10F [41], Na3EuSi6O15·1.47H2O [42] and K3[Gd1-xTbxGe3O8(OH)2] (x = 0, 0.1, 0.3 and 1) [68]. In the particular case of the latter, the room temperature luminescence decay curves confirmed the presence of single Tb3+ site, which is consistent with the Tb3+ location determined by structural analysis [68]. The decay curves detected at the 5D47F5 (Tb3+) transition of K3[Gd1-xTbxGe3O8(OH)2] (x = 0.1 and 0.3) were well fitted by single exponential functions with lifetimes of 2.255 and 2.909 ms for x=0.1 and x=0.3, respectively.

The structure of another strong red emitter Na EuSi O ·1.47H O [42] contains one distinct Eu site, four symmetrically independent Si sites, and three distinct Na sites. It is based on corrugated silicate single layers with the composition [Si2O5] in the ab plane containing 4-, 5-, 6- and 8-membered ring, which are connected via EuO7 polyhedra to form a 3D framework. It contains 4- and 8-membered ring channels along the [100] direction and 5- and 6-membered ring channels along the [001] direction. The charge balancing sodium cations are located in the 6-membered (Na1) and 8- membered ring channels (Na2 and Na3). The photoluminescent studies confirmed the existence of only one Eu3+ local environment, in accordance with the crystallographic results. The room temperature 5D decay curve, detected at the transition of 5D 7F (610 nm) and excitation at 395 nm, can be well fitted by a single exponential function with lifetime of 1.81 ms [42].

Sanjeewa et al. [70] reported the high-temperature hydrothermal synthesis and characterization of a series of new strong red emitters sodium barium rare earth silicates with formula NaBa3Ln3S6O20 (Ln = Y, Nd, Sm, Eu and Gd). Their 3D framework is built from two unique Ln3+ sites, two unique Ba2+ sites and one unique Na+ site, along with two different types of polysilicate building blocks (Si2O7 and Si4O13). A series of channels along the c-axis host the Ba2+ and Na+ ions. Both Ln sites lack symmetry, with Ln1 located at a general position seven-coordinated with oxygen, and Ln2 located at a site having a 2-fold rotational symmetry and eight-coordinated with oxygen. Ln1 and Ln2 polyhedra connect via shared oxygen edges to form infinite chains running parallel to [001] direction. Each Ln2 polyhedron links to four Ln1 polyhedra, essentially forming two zigzag chains. The photoluminescent studies on these europium-containing structures confirmed the presence of two unique Ln3+ sites.

Zhao and co-workers [66] published the preparation of three new silicates containing stoichiometric amounts of lanthanides (K1.25Gd1.25Si2.5O7.5, Cs TbSi O ·2H O and Cs DySi O ) based on anionic silicate chain, layer and framework synthesised under high-temperature and high-pressure conditions. The structure of K1.25Gd1.25Si2.5O7.5 consists of an unusual complex zig-zag silicate chains [Si5O15]10- with 4- and 10-membered rings along [010] direction. One GdO8 polyhedra is connected with four GdO6 octahedra via edge-sharing connection to form a cluster. Such clusters are linked together by Gd-O-Gd bonds to form an infinite chain along the [001] direction. The silicate chains and the gadolinium chains are arranged in parallel directions along the [010] and [001], respectively, and connected by Gd-O-Si bonds to form a three-dimensional framework. The asymmetric unit of K1.25Gd1.25Si2.5O7.5 contains two independent Gd sites (see Table 1), three independent Si sites and four independent K sites. As can be seen in Figure 20 the structure contains 8-membered rings channels along the [001] direction and two kinds of 10-membered rings channels along the [010] and [001] directions, respectively. K1 is located in the 10-membered ring channels while the K2, K3, K4 are located between the gadolinium chains. The structure of Cs TbSi O ·2H O consists of an undulated silicate double layer with 4- and 8-membered rings parallel to the [001] plane, which are built up from cornersharing SiO4 tetrahedra. Such double silicate layers are linked together by TbO6 octahedra via vertex oxygen atoms resulting in a 3D open framework. The asymmetric unit of this material contains one symmetrically independent Tb site (see Table 1), six symmetrically independent Si sites, and four symmetrically independent Cs sites. The structure of this material (Figure 21) contains 8-membered rings channels delimited by SiO4 tetrahedra along [100] and [010] directions, and 6-membered rings delimited by four SiO tetrahedra and two TbO along [010]. The Cs3 cations and the water molecules are located within the former rings, and Cs1 and Cs2 are located near the wall of the last ones. Cs3DySi6O15 is constructed from SiO4 tetrahedra forming a 3D silicate framework [Si O ]6-, which contains 6-membered rings along the [001] as can be seen in the left side of Figure 22. The asymmetric unit contains one symmetrically independent Dy site (see Table 1), one Si site and one Cs site. The Dy is in an octahedral environment, which is connected to six Si atoms coming from two adjacent 6-membered rings via bridging O atoms, while the Si site is in a tetrahedral environment, which is connected to three Si atoms and one Dy atom via oxygen atoms (see the right side of Figure 22). The Cs+ cation is nine-coordinated to the oxygen atoms. Figure 23 shows the photoluminescence spectrum of a pure phase of the Cs3TbSi8O19·2H2O silicate [66]. The preliminary studies showed that it is a roomtemperature green phosphor having strongest 5D 7F transitions at 540 nm and 548 nm, and indicated that the luminescence from higher excited states (e.g. 5D3) was not detectable, implying very efficient nonradiative relaxation to the 5D4 level. The room temperature decay curve of the 5D 7F transition (excited at 266 nm) was well fitted by a single exponential function with a lifetime of 3.11 ms [66].

Wierzbicka-Wieczorek et al. [67] published the results of a crystallographic and photoluminescent study of the microporous mixed-framework silicates Cs1.86K1.14DySi6O15 and (Cs,K)3SmSi6O15 prepared by employment of high-temperature flux mixtures. The asymmetric unit of the former contains three Dy sites, three mixed Cs/Dy sites, five Si sites and fourteen O sites, while the asymmetric unit of the latter contains one Sm site, as well as three Si and nine O sites. Curiously, the authors affirmed that Cs1.86K1.14DySi6O15 has an apparently closely related atomic arrangement in comparison to Cs DySi O [66]. However, they also considered that reported Cs DySi O [66] structure is somewhat doubtful due either to unrecognized twinning or to a wrongly determined unit cell. For instance, differences are observed in the connectivity of Si6O15 rings, which in Cs3DySi6O15 [66] apparently results in the formation of 10-membered rings whereas in Cs K DySi O [67] six irregular 7- membered rings are created. The crystal structure of stoichiometrically identical Cs3EuSi6O15 described by Huang et al. [24] does not involve any relation to the structures discussed above. The photoluminescence studies indicated that both materials suffer self-quenching due to the high concentrations of their lanthanides.

Notwithstanding, the 5D0 decay curves detected in the 5D07F1 and 5D07F2 regions (excited at 532 nm) were well fitted by single exponential functions with a lifetime of 5.45 ± 0.01 ms, confirming the presence of one local Eu3+ environment [24].

Aksenov et al., [48] reported the synthesis of a novel potassium europium silicate, HK6Eu3+[Si10O25] at 500 ºC and total pressure of 1000 atm. Its structure is based on nano-scale oval tubes of 8-membered rings Si O with inner diameters of 1.7 Å and 3.4 Å joint by additional Si-tetrahedra. Symmetrical H-bonds are formed between oxygen atoms along the short diameters of the corrugated 8-membered rings. The room temperature emission spectrum of the solid excited at 337 nm presented the typical sharp emission lines attributed to the transitions between the first excited nondegenerated 5D0 state and the 7F0-4 levels of the fundamental Eu3+ septet. The spectrum did not evidence the luminescence from higher excited states such as 5D , indicating very efficient nonradiative relaxation to the 5D0 level. The 5D0 decay curve recorded at the strongest 7F1 level was well fitted by a single exponential, suggesting the presence of a single Eu3+ environment with a lifetime of 1.169 ± 0.006 ms (see Table 1). Moreover, the relative intensity of the 5D07F1 transition was higher than the 5D07F2 transition, which indicated Eu3+ with a centre of symmetry. However, the resultant quantum yield with the presence of a high Eu concentration and long kinetic attenuation revealed that only a minor number of Eu atoms is in their “luminescent” state. The wide weak resolved lines of 5D 7F transition proposed considerable disorder variation of Eu3+ local environment. Kravtsova et al. [49] published the X-ray spectral diagnosis using this material along with K3Eu3+[Si6O15]·2H2O, K7Sm3[Si12O32], K2Sm[AlSi4O12]·0.375H2O, K4Yb2[Si8O21] and K4Ce2[Al2Si8O24].

The luminescent microporous silicate Na TbSi O ·3H O was synthesized by Wang and co-workers [43] and contains unusual helical sechser silicate chains and 9- membered ring channels. Single-crystal analysis revealed that this material is composed of a macroanionic [TbSi3O9]3- framework with Na+ cations residing in the channels for compensating the negative charges of the structure. Each asymmetric unit contains one crystallographic distinct Tb atom (see Table 1), three crystallographic distinct Si atoms, Na atoms and water molecules. The Tb octahedron shares six oxygen atoms with adjacent Si tetrahedra. This linkage results in a three-dimensional open framework of a microporous terbium(III) silicate which contains 1D 9-membered ring (see Figure 24.a) channels along the [100] direction delimited by four TbO6 octahedra and five SiO tetrahedra with a free aperture of 3.0 Å × 7.1 Å. The connection of the SiO tetrahedra results in an infinite left-handed helical silicate chain with a period of six tetrahedra following the screw axis running along the a-axis (see Figure 24.b). This helical chain has also been found in minerals and synthetic stannosilicates, however, it rarely occurs in the structures of microporous lanthanide silicates. Na1, Na2, O1w and O2w (sodium cations and oxygen atoms from water molecules) reside in the 9-membered rings channels while the Na3 cations are enclosed in the spiral silicate chains and the O3w atoms locate near the spiral silicate chains. The room temperature photoluminescence spectrum of this material [43] in Figure 25 shows several lines between 480 and 650 nm attributed to the 5D47F3-6 transitions of Tb3+ ions. The 5D 7F transitions at 543 and 550 nm are the strongest and the luminescence from higher excited states (e.g. 5D ) is not detectable. Complementarily, the room temperature fluorescence decay curves of the 5D 7F transitions were well fitted by a single-exponential function yielding a life time value of 3.11 ms, which suggested the presence of a single site for Tb3+. This result is in good accordance with the single-crystal structure. The application of these materials in ion exchange was also preliminarily studied. The authors affirmed that the sodium cations can be exchanged by others such as NH +, K+ and Li+. Other lanthanide silicate analogues, for example, Ce, Eu, Er, Sm can also be prepared.

A similar material with general formula Na [Y M Si O ] (M = Tm3+, Tb3+; a = 0-1), an isomorphous multifunctional sodium lanthanide silicate was synthesized by Ananias and co-workers [45]. This material contains yttrium as second rare-earth metal but is possible to obtain others materials, namely Na3(Y,Eu,Tb,Tm)Si3O9, via hydrothermal synthesis, where the judicious choice of the lanthanide cation and its content will allow a remarkably wide-range tuning of the optical properties. For example, the Tbcontaining material synthesized by Ananias et al., [45] has real potential applications in medical diagnostic imaging as X-ray phosphors while the Tm-containing material has a broad room-temperature blue emission with excellent purity. Moreover, it is possible to tune the infrared emission of the Tm-containing material via control of the Y3+/Tm3+ molar ratio.

Na3[(Y,Ln)Si3O9]·3H2O (Ln = Eu, Tb, Er, Ce) are unprecedented chiral microporous lanthanide silicates obtained by Ananias and co-workers [46] as byproducts in the hydrothermal synthesis of dense Na3[LnSi3O9] phosphors [45,115,116]. Before such materials, only two zeolite-type silicates exhibited chiral polymorphism, namely zeolite β and ETS-10, but none are photoluminescent. The photoluminescent spectra of these materials, recorded at 10 K and excited at 526 nm, revealed the presence of a single and low symmetry Eu3+ environment, as indicated by the crystallographic studies but, curiously, when the solid was excited on the ligand-to-Eu3+ charge transfer (CT) band (265 nm) the number of 7F1,2 Stark components doubled, denouncing the existence of two enantiomers in the sample (see Table 1). This was also observed in the 5D0 lifetimes. For instance, at 10 K, the mixed samples Na3[(Y1-

Eu )Si O ]·3H O (with a = 0.2 and 0.3) displayed a similar lifetime (1.59±0.01 ms) for an excitation in the 5D1 level (526 nm) and a strong 7F2 Stark component (608.5 nm). However, different lifetimes were obtained under excitation in the CT band, the sample with a = 0.2 has the same lifetime for the two main 7F Stark components at 607.8 and 609.1 nm (1.48±0.01 ms) while the sample with a = 0.3 displayed different lifetimes (1.39±0.01 and 1.54±0.01 ms) for detection at these wavelengths, respectively. In summary, Ananias and co-workers [46] were able to identify and quantify enantiomeric domains in chiral frameworks through Eu3+ photoluminescence spectroscopy with excitation by unpolarized light in absence of an external magnetic field. The authors indicated this was only possible because they were dealing with extended frameworks (not isolated molecules) that are diastereomeric (‘quasi-enantiomeric’) in long range, but Eu3+ photoluminescence probes essentially local regions around the metal ion, which appears as enantiomeric.

Recently, the same authors reported the synthesis and structural characterization of a similar system, Na3[(Y,Eu)(Si,Ge)3O9]·3H2O, (with Y=0.7-1.0, Eu=0.0-0.3, Ge=0.5- 2.0 and Si=1.0-2.5) exhibiting isomorphic substitution of Si4+ by Ge4+ [47]. Some of the compounds synthesized in the course of this work are isotypical with the rare-earth framework silicates previously reported [46]. As Ge4+ is larger than Si4+ it may also adopt coordination numbers of 5 and 6. Moreover, in a typical tetrahedral coordination, it has larger ionic radius and prefers sites farther from both the charge balancing cations and the framework rare-earth sites available. Moreover, they made clear that Ge4+ seems to have a slight preference for two (T1 and T3) of the three tetrahedra, since T2 (tetrahedra 2 site) is the site closer to Na+ cations and is also the site closer to frameworks rare-earth metal centres. Its inclusion into the tetrahedral sites reduces the rare-earth–oxygen distances and causes a dispersion of local rare-earth sites. The photoluminescence studies indicated that the increasing of the Ge content shifts to lower energy the strongest emission line (5D07F2) and broadens systematically the emission lines, in particular, the 5D07F1,2. The room temperature 5D0 decay curves (excited at 463 nm) were well fitted by single exponential functions (lifetime of 1.44±0.01 ms), supporting the crystallographic evidence for the presence of a single and low symmetry rare-earth (average) environment (see Table 1). The main photoluminescent features of pure Si- [46] and Ge,Si-materials [47] are very similar. Such as in the Ge,Si-materials, quasi-enantiomeric domains were also detected by selective excitation at low temperature (14 K).

The first examples of mixed (up to three) rare-earth gallosilicates, Rb2[REGaSi4O12] with RE3+ = Y3+, Eu3+, Gd3+ and Tb3+, which contain crystallographic independent tetrahedral Ga3+ and Si4+ centres, were synthesized by Lee and co-
# ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT

workers [65]. Their structure encompasses two Rb+ sites, one EuO pentagonal bipyramid, one GaO tetrahedra, and four SiO tetrahedra. The SiO are linked to each other by corner-sharing in a period of eight units along the c-axis, forming unbranched single chains. The previous mentioned GaO tetrahedra are then linked by cornersharing to adjacent silicate chains in two directions (parallel to the a- and b-axes) to form a mixed-anion double layer. Thus, in the bc plane are placed the resulting mixed inorganic double layers composed solely of tetrahedra that have the formula [GaSi4O12]5-. A 3D framework containing two types of 6-membered ring channels parallel to the b-axis is formed due to the fact that each EuO7 polyhedra shares an edge with one SiO4 tetrahedra and corners with one GaO4 and five SiO4. Between the adjacent 6-membered rings, on the periphery of the channels, are located the eightcoordinated Rb+ cations. The photoluminescent studies on Rb [EuGaSi O ] confirmed the presence of one local Eu3+ environment. The decay curves of the 5D 7F and 5D07F2 transitions (excitation at 473 nm) can be well fitted by single exponential functions and lifetime 2.9 ms [65].

In a remarkable work, Ananias et al. [72] reported the preparation of a lanthanide silicate Na[(Gd Eu )SiO ] (x = 0.01, 0.1, 0.4 and 1) that exhibits uncommon photoluminescence properties due to structural disorder and a phase transition. The crystal structure determined at 100 K contains one Gd site, one Eu site, one Na site, one Si site and three distinct oxygen sites. The structural disorder associated with the SiO 4- building unit results in various local environments with subtle differences in the first coordination sphere, confirmed by the dispersion of bond lengths and angles. At lower temperatures (30 K) this structural disorder seems fade away, giving a bodycentered unit cell to the centrosymmetric orthorhombic material. With this symmetry the disordered tetrahedral SiO44- building unit and the charge-balancing Na+ cation occupy, in the same unit cell, almost the same average crystallographic positions. On the other hand, the Gd and Eu seem to be sixteen-coordinated. The introduction of Tb3+, e.g. Na[(Gd1-x-yEuxTby)SiO4], provides an unprecedented example of a photoluminescent ratiometric thermometer. The temperature sensing capability is due to the temperature dependence of the Tb3+-to-Eu3+ energy transfer. In fact, increasing the temperature promotes such energy transfer, with respective evolution of the emission colour from yellow at 12 K (Tb3+ plus Eu3+ emission) to red (mostly Eu3+ emission). The absolute temperature measurement was inferred via the integrated intensity ratio of the 5D 7F (Tb3+) and 5D07F4 (Eu3+). The 5D4 decay curves at 12 K (excitation at 483.5 nm) yielded lifetimes of 1.94 ± 0.02 ms (0.90 ± 0.03 ms at 296 K) and 2.50 ± 0.01 (2.38 ± 0.03 ms at 296 K) ms, for Na[(Gd0.9Tb0.1)SiO4] and Na[(Gd0.8Eu0.1Tb0.1)SiO4],
respectively [72]. This peculiar feature was also observed recently in a luminescent metal–organic framework thermometer studied by Wu et al. [117].

Abeysinghe and co-workers [73] just reported the preparation of a new lanthanide mixed-valent vanadium(III/IV) oxosilicates crystallizing in a quasi 2D rutile-based structure and whose formula is Ln V Zn Si O (Ln = La, Ce, Pr, and Nd). The metallic Zn(II) was used to reduce in situ the vanadium(V) to vanadium(III/IV) through a hightemperature molten salt method. The extended 3D structure of this material is composed by two 2D sheets of edge- and face-shared LnO polyhedra, edge-shares VO6 octahedra and Si2O7 groups. Two crystallographic unique Ln centres, Ln1 and Ln2, are located in an irregular nine-coordinated polyhedron. Curiously, they form a [Ln(1)Ln(2)O ] dimer that also shares four edges with other four dimers to create a lanthanide oxide layer parallel to the ab plane. On the other hand, there are also a 2D vanadium silicate that contains mixed Zn/V octahedra linked by Si O groups and a 2D vanadium oxide layer that is best described as a rutile-like arrangement, both parallel to the ab plane. The authors also claimed that the first cerium-containing vanadium silicate was prepared during their work, Ce4V4.77Zn0.23Si4O22.

In the investigation towards the preparation of Eu2+-containing barium borates and barium borosilicates in apatite and related phases [60], Heyward and co-workers [71] prepared NaBaEuSi3O9, NaBa3Eu3Si6O20 and BaEu6(Si3B6O24)(OH)2. The latter is related to the rare and poorly understood mineral cappelenite whose chemical formula is Ba(Y,RE)6(Si3B6O24)F2. NaBaEuSi3O9 has a complex 3D framework comprising puckered Si3O9 cyclosilicate ring as building blocks connected to each other through the sodium, europium and barium. Na atoms are positioned in a distorted sevencoordinated environment and linked to three Si3O9 rings, while Ba is eight-coordinated and providing connections to six Si3O9 rings. Eu is six-coordinated with oxygen and forms a slightly distorted octahedron. NaBa3Eu3Si6O20 possesses two distinct and independent silicate arrangements as Si4O13 and Si2O7, and thus the structural formula is NaBa3Eu3(Si4O13)(Si2O7). The former arrangement is interesting because it occurred as an isolated island and not as a typical finite chain. The latter groups occur in common isolated pyrosilicate Si2O7 arrangement. These silicate building blocks are linked to the barium, europium and sodium to form a complex 3D framework. Na is in a six-coordinated distorted pentagonal-pyramidal geometry by sharing two edges with a single Si2O7 group, one edge with a Si4O13 group, and a corner with one of the apical oxygen atoms of a second Si4O13 group. Eu and Ba are seven- and eight-coordinated. The former is in a pentagonal bipyramid (Eu1) and a square antiprism (Eu2), while the latter takes a trigonal prism (Ba1) and a distorted cube (Ba2) form. BaEu6(Si3B6O24)(OH)2 is formed by tetrahedral borate and silicate building blocks. Six borate groups form B O rings that connect to one another by B-O-Si-O-B corner sharing through the SiO4 tetrahedra, and thus forming the overall Si3B6O24 borosilicate sheet with two types of channels along the ab plane. Twelve-coordinated barium and eight-coordinated europium form a layer of their own, alternating with the borosilicate sheet along the c-axis. The latter form edge-sharing clusters of EuO7(OH) along the caxis by sharing three edges and a OH group. No photoluminescent studies were reported.
## 3.2.2. Layered lanthanide silicates

In order to study the evolution of photoluminescence across dimensionality in lanthanide silicates, Kostova and co-workers reported the photoluminescence of layered lanthanide silicates [18,19,118]. Such materials combine the properties of layered silicates (intercalation chemistry) or zeolites (such as ion exchange and molecular sieve) and photoluminescence [119]. Ananias et al., [20] reported the hydrothermal synthesis and structural characterization of layered lanthanide silicates, K3[M1-aLnaSi3O8(OH)2] (M = Y3+, Tb3+ ; Ln = Er3+, Eu3+, Tb3+ and Gd3+ ; a ≤ 1) named AV-22 materials. The structure of Ln-AV-22 contains a single crystallographic Ln3+ centre (a slightly disorder LnO6 octahedra) coordinated to six SiO4 tetrahedra. There are two distinct silicon tetrahedra: (i) SiO4H establishes corner-sharing bridges between adjacent LnO6 octahedra, leading to the formation of one-dimensional arrays running the c-axis direction and (ii) SiO4 units that share corners with two SiO4H tetrahedra and two LnO6 octahedra that links adjacent one-dimensional arrays and leads to the formation of a two-dimensional [LnSi3O8(OH)2]n3n- anionic perforated plane perpendicular to [010] containing 3- and 7-membered rings. Figure 26 shows that there are also two crystallographic sites for the potassium cations: K1 resides within the pores (see Figure 26.b) of the anionic perforated plane while K2 occupies the interlayer space (Figure 26.a). The structure of these materials permits the inclusion of different (a second or even a third) Ln3+ cation in one solid and, therefore, allows the fine-tuning of their photoluminescent properties (see Table 1). These layered lanthanide silicate structures were found to be identical to that of the analogues materials containing Ho3+ and Y3+ previously reported by Ponomarev et al., [120] and Filipenko et al., [121], respectively. Ananias et al., [20] affirmed that the Er-AV-22 material is a roomtemperature infrared phosphor, while Tb- and Eu-AV-22 are visible emitters. Moreover, they also reported that for mixed Tb3+/Eu3+ materials, the incorporation of Eu cations in the interlayer space by replacing potassium cations allows the activation of Tb3+-to-Eu3+ energy transfer. They were surprised when they assisted that phenomenon because the Tb3+-to-Eu3+ energy transfer between optical centres was unlikely since few Ln3+ were present, and thus were far apart, being located essentially in the interlayer. Consequently, the authors affirmed that such mechanisms may be tuned by judicious choice of the Ln3+ cations and by the occupancy of the layer and interlayer metal sites.

Kostova and co-workers [118] published the synthesis and structural characterization of photoluminescent layered Y(III) and Tb(III) silicates (AV-22) containing Ce(III) and found energy transfer mechanisms for mixed Tb/Ce-AV-22, which allowed the fine-tuning of the colour emission in the blue-green region. Although the emission radiance is higher in the pure Tb-AV-22, upon Ce3+ excitation the emission radiance of Tb/Ce-AV-22 is approximately 2 times higher than that measured under direct Tb3+ excitation. In further research [18,19], Kostova et al., reported the AV-23 materials, K3[MSi3O9] (M = Y3+, Tb3+), from calcination of the layered AV-22, K3[MSi3O8(OH)2] (M = Y3+, Tb3+), at approximately 650 ºC and compared the photoluminescence features of both. The crystal structure of AV-22 may be described as the parallel packing of the [LnSi3O8(OH)2]n3n- anionic layers in the [ABAB...] fashion along the b-axis. The anionic layers are interconnected through strong OH···O hydrogen bounds between neighbouring Si-OH groups. Figure 27 is the schematic representation of the transformation process of AV-22 into AV-23. The dehydration of AV-22 material causes the disorder condensation of the adjacent [LnSi3O8(OH)2]n3nlayers yielding AV-23. Similar to Ln-AV-22, the structure of Ln-AV-23 contains a single crystallographically independent Ln3+ metal centre coordinated to six SiO4 tetrahedra in a distorted octahedral geometry. Individual LnO octahedra are isolated from each other by wollastonite-type siliceous chains, [Si6O17]n10n-, running parallel to the a-axis. The anionic [LnSi3O9]n3n- framework is characterized by a three channel system, filled with highly disordered potassium cations, with the main tunnels running parallel to [100] and [010]. One main difference between AV-22 and AV-23 materials is the type of channels. The 7-membered pores in the layer of AV-22 align upon condensation in the a-axis of AV-23. The condensation also generates more regular channels with 8- membered elliptical rings with a cross section of ca. 2.0 Å × 4.0 Å. The photoluminescence studies revealed interesting results. Although the crystal structures of these materials exhibited the presence of a single independent Ln3+ environment, two or three Ln3+ local environments were found. The existence of two peaks in the 5D07F0 transition revealed the presence of, at least, two distinct Eu3+ environments (inset in Figure 28). They were further investigated by recording their decay curves on the 7F0-2 levels as a function of the excitation wavelength (392 or 463 nm). The data can be well fitted by biexponential functions when monitoring at the maximum of the 5D07F1,2 transitions (lifetimes detected at 609.5 nm and 300 K were 2.02 ± 0.02 ms and 0.58 ± 0.01 ms) and three exponential functions when monitoring both at the maximum of the 5D07F0 transition and at the low-energy side of the 5D07F2 transitions (lifetimes detected at 615 nm and 300 K were 2.13 ± 0.03 ms, 1.25 ± 0.02 ms and 0.33 ± 0.01 ms), confirming the existence of two or three Ln3+ sites (see Table 1). Those two or three lanthanide sites can lie on the metal centres in regular framework positions, defect regions and also micropores, replacing potassium cations. Kostova and co-workers [18,19] also reported that the calcination made on the AV-22 yielding the AV-23 material increases the intensity of the Ln3+ emission due to the removing of OH groups but also increases the importance of the Ln3+-Ln3+ interactions as a quenching emission channel. Thus, Kostova et al., [19] affirmed that the photoluminescent properties may be adjusted by changing the dimensionality of the layered lanthanide silicates.

Wang and co-workers [44] synthesized and characterized 2D layered lanthanide germanates with tunable photoluminescent properties. The four 2D compounds K [Tb Eu Ge O (OH) ] (x = 1, 0.88, 0.67, 0), denoted as TbGeO-JU-87, Tb0.88Eu0.12GeO-JU-87, Tb0.67Eu0.33GeO-JU-87 and TbGeO-JU-87, are structurally analogous to the lanthanide silicates previously described by Ananias et al., [20]. Here, similarly to that reported by Ananias and co-workers for lanthanide silicates, their optical properties are also tunable. For instance, their emission colour shifts closer to red region when increasing the Eu3+ content whereas Tb0.67Eu0.33GeO-JU-87 has a higher Tb3+-to-Eu3+ energy transfer efficiency than Tb Eu GeO-JU-87.

The room temperature decay curves of the 5D07F2 transitions (613 nm) 5D47F5 transitions (540 nm) of EuGeO-JU-87 and TbGeO-JU-87 can be well fitted by a single exponential function, yielding lifetimes of 0.84 ms and 1.02 ms, which suggested a single Eu3+ and Tb3+ environment, respectively [44]. The energy transfer in Tb Eu GeO-JU-87 and Tb Eu GeO-JU-87 was assessed by both Eu3+ and Tb3+ decay curves. Their Tb3+ decay curves detected at 5D47F5 transitions (540 nm) were well fitted by single exponential function, yielding lifetimes of 0.18 and 0.07 ms, respectively, which are much shorter than that of TbGeO-JU-87 (1.02 ms) due to the contribution of Tb3+ as a donor in energy transfer [44]. On the other hand, their Eu3+ decay curves were well fitted by biexponential functions, being however composed by a rise time (instead of a decay time), which also confirmed the existence of energy transfer in the two compounds [44]. The average rise and decay times related to the fitted function were 0.0567 and 0.4941 ms for Tb0.88Eu0.12GeO-JU-87 and 0.0287 and 0.4860 ms for Tb0.67Eu0.33GeO-JU-87, which means that the rise time decreases with increasing Eu3+ concentration, implying that the rate of Tb3+-to-Eu3+ energy transfer is dependent on the Eu3+ concentration [44].

Liu et al. [68] also reported a material similar to that described by Ananias et al. [20]. Nonetheless the new lanthanide germinates family K3[TbxGd1-xGe3O8(OH)2] (x = 1, 0.3, 0.1, 0) was synthesized hydrothermally at 400 ºC and 100 MPa. Their optical properties were also presented as being tunable.

In order to implant the lanthanide silicates described previously [18,20,118,119] in sensors and other devices, it is of interest to prepare nanoparticles of these materials, which could be used, for example, in ink-jet printing or incorporated in polymer matrixes [21]. Following this reasoning, Ananias and co-workers [21] published the synthesis of the first example of nanoparticles (with particle size range of 20-40 nm) of pure layered Ln2(SiO4H)(OH)2(H2O)Cl where Ln = Eu, Gd and Tb and of mixed microcrystalline layered Ln silicates containing different Eu3+/Gd3+ and Tb3+/Gd3+ ratios. They are unique because they are the first stoichiometric layered silicates containing chloride in the coordination sphere of a single lanthanide ion. The structure of Eucontaining material is constructed by parallel packing along [100] of two-dimensional undulated layers placed in the bc plane (see Figure 29). The crystal structure contains two crystallographically independent Eu3+ centres, Eu1 and Eu2, respectively EuO and EuO Cl, which are significantly distorted due to the structural features of the layer. Eu1 and Eu2 are not located at the crystallographic inversion centres however the first coordination sphere of Eu1 is approximately centrosymmetric. Tetrahedra of SiO4H bridges six neighbouring lanthanide centres leading to relatively long Eu-O distance, 2.60 Å and 2.48 Å for Eu1 and Eu2, respectively. Therefore, the Ln3+ coordination geometries are best described as a distorted tricapped trigonal prism for Eu1 and as distorted dodecahedra for Eu2. Furthermore, Eu1 is coordinated to a water molecule while Eu2 interacts instead with a Cl- anion. The neighbouring layers interactions are assured by a network of hydrogen bonds involving the terminal Si-OH group, the coordinated water molecule and Cl- anion. The photoluminescence studies showed that these materials display interesting and tuneable photoluminescence properties, such as energy transfer between the pairs Eu3+/Gd3+ and Tb3+/Gd3+. Even more important, this material may be explored for sensing F- and Cl- ions, since the photoluminescence properties of the mixed Eu3+/Gd3+ sample change upon F- for Cl- ion exchange. Figure 30 shows the emission spectra of the Eu-containing materials. The presence of two lines for the nondegenerated 5D07F0 transition and the local-field splitting of the 7F1 level in six Stark components suggest the presence of two different Eu3+ environments (Table 1), which is in accordance with the crystal structure. The 5D decay curves of (EuxGd1-x)2(SiO4H)(OH)2(H2O)Cl recorded at 5D07F1 transition (590.2 nm for Eu1 and 586.8 nm for Eu2) with excitation at 393 nm were well fitted by single exponential functions, indicating the presence of two Eu3+ sites: 0.216 ± 0.001 ms and 0.206 ±

0.002 ms for x = 1.0, 0.341 ± 0.002 ms and 0.333 ± 0.003 ms for x = 0.5, and 0.356 ± 0.003 ms and 0.415 ± 0.003 ms for x = 0.125 [21]. It is worth mentioning that the difference between lifetimes are more pronounced for x = 0.125 [21]. Several other lanthanide silicates with the Cl- ions interacting with four or more Ln3+ centres are known [122–124].

Another way to implant Ln-silicates in sensors and other devices is the direct preparation of films. Microporous ETS-10 thick films have been in-situ hydrothermally synthesized on α-alumina and stainless substrates, and Eu3+ was introduced into pore by ion exchange [125]. The photoluminescence excitation spectra indicate that unlike powdered samples, where direct Eu3+ excitation is comparable to excitation sensitized via lattice energy levels, the latter process largely dominates in films. Only a single Eu3+ site is detected in films, even at relatively high Eu3+ contents (Ti/Eu = 6.5).
## Conclusions

The research on new materials is very often motivated by an attempt to discover mineral structures provided by Nature. Then, with the objective to tune and improve their properties, researchers tailor the parent/native solids, for instance, by introducing heteroatoms in their frameworks. This approach brought to light new molecular architectures and has broadened the knowledge about the chemistry of microporous zeolite-type materials.

Recently, novel studies have been dedicated to the incorporation of rare earth (in particular lanthanide) elements in the pores or framework of zeolite-type materials. Such RE/Ln-containing materials have revealed their potential multi-functionality, since they can combine, in a single and stable solid, microporosity and tuneable optical properties. Furthermore, like the majority of zeolites, they are thermally and chemically stable. Due to these reasons the materials appear as excellent candidates for use in various areas, such as, optoelectronics and nonlinear optics, magnetic materials, sensors and other nanotechnology devices. In addition, their application as ion exchangers should be pointed out because they may play an important role in water treatment and environmental control.

The study of the influence of molecules or ionic species sorbed by RE/Lnsilicates upon their optical properties is a very promising field of research that may be exploited with interest in the near future. This topic was very recently pursued with Eu-AV-20 and Tb/Eu-AV-9 that were tested as Cs+ exchangers and sensors. Actually, ion exchange is an excellent method to modify the structural dimensionality of Lnstructures, where layered solids should deserve special attention. Taking into account the space between adjacent layers can host different ions, it may be modified, which may cause relevant changes in the photoluminescence spectra.

The introduction of a second Ln-emitter also opens the possibility for fine-tuning light-emission properties, as in the case of Tb/Eu-AV-9. This feature may be of capital importance since this second lanthanide may act as a luminescent centre (increasing the distance or promoting energy transfer between Ln3+ ions) or activate (protect) the framework lanthanide. Sometimes the second Ln-emitter is a result of a structural disorder, as is the case of Eu-AV-20, where, besides the regular Ln centres of the framework, others are disordered over the sodium cation sites.

Besides the hydrothermal synthesis of rare earth silicates, the recent years were profitable on the preparation of new rare earth silicates through different approaches, namely via high-temperature high-pressure hydrothermal and flux processes. In some specific cases of the former, a two-step mechanism firstly grants a glass that is then used as feedstock in the hydrothermal reaction, which generally may lead to the preparation of multiple crystal phases, as assisted for some barium borosilicates. On the other hand, the flux method may be of interest since it essentially prevents the presence of water molecules that often jeopardize the photoluminescence properties due to quenching effects.
