## Abstract

A large number of silicates containing transition metals and rare earth (in particular lanthanide) elements have been reported until recently. Generally, they exhibit a rich structural chemistry with interesting physical and chemical properties, and, in contrast to zeolites, which are built of [SiO ]4- and [AlO ]5- tetrahedrons, their frameworks embody metals in different coordination. In particular, materials containing rare earth and/or lanthanide elements may combine, in a single and stable solid, microporosity and tuneable optical properties. Such multifunctionality may be explored with interest, being a challenging approach to novel chemical and optical applications.

This article aims to review rare earth and lanthanide silicates published to date, namely their relevant structure features and photoluminescent properties, being divided in two sections according to the major approaches used for their preparation, i.e. doping and embedding. The parent materials hosting the rare earth or lanthanide elements, the type and number of such emitters, and the disorder and dimensionality of the solids are some of the addressed topics. Furthermore, this review is also intended to highlight the great challenges that optical centres design offers in the field of materials science. Some potential applications are also debated, such as wastewater remediation, nuclear medicine, imaging, and sensors. Notwithstanding the relevance that photoluminescent porous and layered lanthanide silicates may achieve in wastewater treatment, as a result of their stability and high selectivity combined with capacity, their sensing ability towards a specific ion or molecule will be for sure of capital importance in the near future.
## 1. Introduction

Zeolites and zeolitic materials, like aluminophosphates (AlPOs), silicoaluminophospates (SAPOs) and metalaluminophosphates (MeAPOs), have crystalline open-framework structures assembled from tetrahedral units interconnected to each other by sharing all the oxygen atoms to form intracrystaline hollow spaces and channels of molecular dimensions. Zeolites are aluminosilicates built of [SiO ]4- and [AlO ]5-, and the negative charge of the framework is balanced by a range of extra-framework cations, which render them ion exchange properties. When the [SiO4]4- is substituted by [PO4]3- tetrahedra, aluminophosphates known as AlPOs are originated. Furthermore, the addition of another element to the aluminophosphate frameworks, for example, Si, metal ions Mg, Co, Mn, Fe, as well as others, led to the silicoaluminophosphate and metalloaluminophosphate families, SAPO and MeAPO, respectively. AlPO frameworks have no net charge and so they possess little catalytic potential and no cation exchange ability [1]. Although the briefly described structures of the previous zeolites and zeolitic materials are all based on tetrahedral building units, some others microporous structures like manganese oxides with entirely octahedral framework atoms have also been reported [2].

The main aspect to retain in this context is the possibility of constructing materials based on heteropolyhedras, such as octahedra, pentahedra and tetrahedra (OPT). The OPT materials [3,4] are not simply an interesting addition of zeotype solids, since they have been investigated for over 25 years and already include more than one hundred different entities with new properties. In the last decade, much research was developed on the syntheses of materials comprising transition metals and rare earth (RE) (especially lanthanides, Ln) guests in mixed OPT microporous silicates hosts. The latter one is attracting much interest due to their optical properties and was reviewed in 2003 by Rocha and Carlos [5], in 2005 by Rocha and Lin [6] and in 2013 by Rocha et al. [7]. The preparation of zeotype Ln-silicates is an emerging field since the beginning of this century, though they are being essentially investigated as phosphor materials and as probes to obtain information about the structure and environment inside the cages where cations are located [8,9]. Nevertheless, they can combine, in a single and stable crystalline structure, microporosity and tuneable optical properties, which makes them interesting materials for potential applications in many devices, for example in cathode ray tubes, projection televisions, fluorescent tubes and X-ray detectors, and in photonics and optical communications [10]. Moreover, recently, considerable attention has been given to them since they can play an important role in the field of wastewater remediation as inorganic exchangers with sensing ability to cations [11–13].

The lanthanide series comprises fifteen chemical elements with atomic numbers 57 through 71, from lanthanum to lutetium. The fifteen lanthanides, along with chemically similar scandium and yttrium, are often collectively known as rare earth elements, and all of them form (at least) trivalent cations, hereafter denoted by Ln3+. Materials that contain lanthanide elements can emit over the entire spectral range: near infrared (Nd3+, Er3+), red (Eu3+, Pr3+, Sm3+), green (Er3+, Tb3+), and blue (Tm3+, Ce3+) [14]. Their optical transitions occur only between 4f orbitals, which are well shielded from their chemical environment by 5s2 and 5p6 electrons and, as a consequence, atomic-like emission spectra displaying characteristic sharp lines may be observed [5]. However, the emission spectrum of a given material may be influenced by the presence of neighbouring molecules and/or ions, and thus the possibility to sense their presence in the matrix may be explored with interest. The change of photoluminescence response induced by ions sorption has been recently investigated for sensing purposes [11–13], while the entrapment of molecular species in zeolitic cavities acting as luminescence centres or activators of the framework Ln3+ ions has not been yet pursued.

To introduce lanthanide ion centres into microporous silicates there are at least two possible ways [5,6]. One way is to ion exchange the Na+ and K+ located inside the pores of the pre-synthesized material by Ln3+ cations. Another way is to embed the Ln3+ cations in the microporous framework, resulting in silicates that contain stoichiometric amounts of these elements. This approach was described in detail firstly by Rocha and Carlos [5] in 2003. There are also two other feasible ways of hosting lanthanide luminescent centres in microporous materials, namely, by enclosing lanthanide complexes with organic ligands in zeolitic open spaces and coordinating organic species to metal frameworks (Porous Coordination Polymers – PCPs – and Metal-Organic Frameworks – MOFs) [15,16]. This review will focus on inorganic materials, especially metal and lanthanide silicates, and therefore those two other approaches will not be discussed here.

The aim of this article is to review the structure and associated photoluminescent properties of lanthanide materials. The principal structures of Ln-silicates reviewed in this paper are resumed in Table 1, which contains their general formulas and, when possible, their names and mineral analogues. It is also indicated how many RE/Ln sites the structure possesses, since it is an important feature for these classes of materials.

The review is divided as follows: The general introduction (Section 1) that finishes with the relevance of the article (Section 1.1); The main contents of the review are presented and discussed in Section 2, namely: Materials doped with lanthanides via ion exchange (postsynthesis; Section 2.1), and Lanthanide silicates (Section 2.2). The last one is split into microporous (Section 2.2.1) and layered (Section 2.2.2) lanthanide silicates.

The zeolitic materials were included in Section 2.1 since they play a chief role in catalysis. In fact, most of these family members have a significant position in several applications where the light emission is one of the less explored. Moreover, it is important to realize that if it is feasible to incorporate lanthanides as part of extra-framework cations in a structure, these lightemitting ions may turn possible to understand the distribution and coordination of other ions/molecules in aluminosilicates. An example that confirms the relevance of zeolites as light emitters is the case of zeolite NaY, a microporous aluminosilicate that has hydrated Ln3+ ions in its large cavities; more specifically, Gadolite, a Gd3+ modified zeolite NaY that possesses great potential as magnetic resonance imaging contrast agents [17].

The lanthanide silicates are divided into microporous and layered solids. The main purpose of focusing such layered materials separately is to show that they gave an important contribution to the study of the evolution of photoluminescence across Ln-containing silicates dimensionality [18,19]. In other words, it is intended to explain that by changing the structural dimensionality of lanthanide (or transition metal) materials it is possible to tune their lightemission properties. Hence, if it is of interest to use them as sensors and other devices, layered lanthanide silicate nanoparticles may also be explored.
## 1.1. Relevance of the review

Since RE/Ln-silicates combine in a single and stable solid microporosity and tuneable optical properties, it is important to keep seeking for applications where optical features may be of interest. In this context, ion exchange and adsorption appear as valuable applications, since the uptake of ions or molecules by such materials may produce measurable differences on its photoluminescent spectra and thus making them promising chemical sensors. Nonetheless, it is important to know in advance the number of RE/Ln sites optically available in each material (see Table 1). Sorption processes may be even more relevant when the solid has a layered structure, since the space between adjacent layers can host different ions or molecules that may act as Ln-antennae or efficient energy bridges across them [20]. This was clearly observed in the photoluminescence studies accomplished by Ananias et al., [21], where energy transfer was detected between different lanthanide centres of the pure layered Ln2(SiO4H)(OH)2(H2O)Cl. Additionally, the sorbed solutes (ions or molecules) may modify the interlayer space which also causes differences upon the photoluminescent spectra. For instance, Ananias et al., [21] revealed that the photoluminescent properties of a mixed Ln-silicate may change upon F-/Cl- ion exchange.

Another interesting strategy is the use of materials containing mixed valence lanthanides (e.g. Ce(III)/Ce(IV)) as exchangers. For example, Jeong et al., [22] suggested that when Ce(IV) content increased, less extra-framework cations were required to balance the charge of the anionic framework, and thus modified its sorption characteristics.

The modification of the disorder and defects of a solid framework can be also an interesting route to tune the light emission of RE/Ln-containing materials. For instance, a solid may contain one regular framework emitter (Ln1) and one emitter polyhedron (Ln2) disordered over other element site that is optically independent and consequently detectable [23]. This may be a relevant feature if one of the optical sites is exchangeable, since its concentration determines the light emission spectra of the solid.

Recently, microporous Eu-AV-20 was proved to be very effective for sensing the uptake of Cs+ from aqueous solutions [12,13]. The exchange is detectable on the emission spectra of the solid (as can be seen in Figure 1), mainly in the first three transitions – 5D07F0, 5D07F1 and 5D07F2 – proving that Eu-AV-20 emits differently depending on the vicinity of the Eu3+. The obtained results revealed that the Cs+ concentration in the solid affects the intensity of one or more transitions of the spectra. Similar studies were carried out with the mixed lanthanide silicate Tb/Eu-AV-9 [11].

In general, sorption processes present a well-known limitation to the chemical sensing ability of RE/Ln-silicates, and this fact requires some cautions. Water may quench the photoluminescent emission and disguise the real influence of the sorbed species upon the 2D or 3D structure, therefore the water content of the solid should be known in order to avoid misconceptions.
## 2. Lanthanide Materials
## 2.1. Materials doped with lanthanides via ion exchange

A lanthanide-doped material is a solid whose original extra-framework cations were exchanged by Ln3+ ions. After ion exchange, the material can be also submitted to a calcination, which may produce denser phases and intensify the emission of the lanthanide, suppressing the quenching effect caused by the presence of water within the channels of the solid. This procedure is useful for understanding the distribution and the coordination of some cations and/or water molecules within the pores of the solids.

In order to investigate the distribution and coordination of the lanthanides cations in MFI zeolites, such as ZSM-5, Tiseanu and co-workers [32] reported the synthesis, characterization and photoluminescence studies of Tb3+-doped microporousmesoporous zeolite-1 materials. Some previous studies involving the time-resolved photoluminescence characterization of Eu3+-doped ZSM-5 found that the europium coordination number in ZSM-5 is smaller than in water, due to the displacement of solvent molecules around it by the framework oxygen atoms [74]. Moreover, from the intrazeolitic redox process of Ce3+-Ce4+ or from FT-IR studies it was also possible to collect information related to the location of cerium and lanthanum cations in ZSM-5 [75]. Additionally, density functional calculations showed that these lanthanum cations are favourably accommodated on the walls of the straight 10-membered ring channels of ZSM-5 [8,9], where they are coordinated to six oxygen atoms, four from the zeolite framework and two from the hydrolysis of lanthanide hydrate. In the work of Tiseanu et al., [32] the doping was accomplished by adding 1 g of zeolite-1 fresh material to an aqueous solution of Tb3+ and stirring it for 30 min at 80 ºC. As can be seen in Figure 2, the presence of one and two peaks in the most intense 5D47F5 transition of the photoluminescence spectra indicated the existence of one and two chemical environments for the hydrated Tb3+-zeolite-1 and for its calcined form, respectively (see Table 1). Furthermore, terbium in the hydrated Tb3+-zeolite-1 is found as a single specie with lifetime between 0.45 and 0.57 ms, while in its calcined form the two environments have different lifetimes between 0.6-1.0 ms and 1.6-2.0 ms.

One of the first materials to be doped with lanthanides via ion exchange was ETS-10 (Engelhard TitanoSilicate number 10), an interesting material belonging to the family of crystalline microporous titanosilicates. ETS-10 [(Na,K)2Si5TiO13·xH2O] is considered the most important OPT material because it was the precursor of most of the latter work in the OPT field since it has no mineral equivalent and to solve its structure much studies were necessary. It was firstly prepared at Engelhard

Corporation, and its structure was solved and briefly reported by Anderson et al., [76– 78]. It comprises corner-sharing SiO4 tetrahedra and TiO6 octahedra linked through bridging oxygen atoms. Although many ordered variants of ETS-10 exist (some of which are chiral), ETS-10 can display a considerable degree of disorder, which is manifested as a displacement of adjacent sheets along [110] (i.e., always 1/4 unit cell along [100] and 1/4 unit cell along [010]) [76]. The stacking sequences of the ETS-10 sheets can explain all possible ordered and disordered polytypes of ETS-10, and the nature of their defects. The two end polytypes are: 1) polytype A with chiral symmetry comprising a stacking sequence that results in a zig-zag arrangement of 12-ring pores; and 2) polytype B (see Figure 3) with a diagonal arrangement of 12-ring pores caused by a different stacking sequence [76]. The -2 charge caused by every framework titanium is compensated by extra-framework cations, usually Na+ and K+. This material, which presents a considerable potential for applications like shape-selective catalysis and ion exchange, was doped with erbium and europium by Rocha et al., [30] and Rainho et al., [28,29], respectively. Both Eu3+- and Er3+-doped ETS-10 were calcined in air at 1073 K, which made them undergo a phase change into synthetic narsarsukite [(Na,K)2TiS4O11], displaying high and stable room-temperature emission spectra in the visible and infrared regions.

The tetragonal titanosilicate narsarsukite was found in alkali pegmatites in Narsarsuk, Greenland, and is made up of rings of four SiO4 tetrahedra linked by cornersharing TiO octahedra chains. The cavities between the SiO tubes and the octahedra chains contain only Na+ in the mineral. Eu3+-doped ETS-10 can be transformed into narsarsukite to improve photoluminescence efficiency, because the presence of a significant number of water molecules inside the pores of ETS-10, which coordinate to the lanthanide cation, partially quench the emission process, and thus reduce the photoluminescence. The same happens with Er3+-doped ETS-10 where no optical activity was detected. Therefore, one way to circumvent such partial or total photoluminescence quenching by water molecules and hydroxyl ions consisted in collapsing the microporous framework of those materials into more dense ones. In this transformation process, the lanthanide cations were trapped in the narsarsukite lattice and its amount was easily controlled by fine-tuning the previous ion exchange. Figure 4 shows the obtained emission spectra of Eu3+-doped ETS-10 and Eu3+-doped narsarsukite. Rainho et al., [28,29] unequivocally indicated that there are more than one local Eu3+ environment in these titanosilicates (see Table 1) and that this can be clearly determined from the presence of, at least, two distinct 5D07F0 transitions.

In an attempt to improve the luminescence efficiency obtained with the Ln-doped titanosilicate ETS-10, Rainho et al., [31] made similar studies on a synthetic umbite (a microporous zirconium silicate K2ZrSi3O9·H2O), whose doping procedure was exactly the same. The zirconium silicate was doped with the lanthanide (Eu3+) via conventional ion exchange and calcined in air at high temperature (in this case at 1373 K) during 12 hours. Once again the main purpose of the calcination was to prepare a denser structure that, in this case, is analogue of the mineral wadeite. Both doped zirconium silicates displayed a high and stable room temperature emission in the visible spectral region. Furthermore, the emission spectra recorded for Eu3+-doped wadeite and for Eu3+-doped umbite indicated the presence of two and one optically active europium environments, respectively (see Table 1). This is observed in the nondegenerated 5D07F0 transition (see Figure 5), where the appearance of one and two peaks indicated the presence of one and two optically active centres. In accordance with this result, the 5D0 decay curves detected for the 5D07F2 (613 nm) can be well fitted by single and biexponential functions for the Eu3+-doped umbite and Eu3+-doped wadeite, respectively. The former had a lifetime of 0.35 ± 0.01 ms at 14 K (0.15 ± 0.01 ms at 300 K), while the latter had lifetimes of 0.71 ± 0.01 ms and 1.89 ± 0.02 at 14 K (0.20 ± 0.01 ms and 1.49 ± 0.02 ms at 300 K). However, the authors referred that although the umbite structure has two potassium sites, only the one located in the relatively large 8- membered rings can be ion exchanged by Eu3+ ions. Curiously, the synthetic wadeite possesses only one potassium site but two local environments appeared for Eu3+ ions. The possible explanation for such phenomenon is that europium ions could belong to a centre A, in a local environment that is less covalent (replacing K+), or to a centre B, located in a more covalent environment caused by the substitution of Zr4+ framework ions. This is confirmed by the different lifetimes of Eu3+. Concerning the luminescence efficiency, the authors also indicated that qualitatively the luminescence of Eu3+-doped umbite (with a Zr/Eu molar ratio ca. 10) is higher than Eu3+-doped ETS-10 (Ti/Eu = 10), since the number of water molecules inside the pores of their fully hydrated native forms are one and four, respectively.

Rainho and co-workers [79] reported the synthesis and the photoluminescence properties of Eu3+-doped narsarsukite (Na4(Ti,Fe)2[Si8O20](O,OH,F)2) prepared by the sol-gel process. One of the main purposes of this work was to reduce the amount of siliceous impurities detected in a previous Eu3+-doped narsarsukite obtained by calcination of an ion exchanged precursor, the Eu3+-ETS-10 [28,29]. However, the Eu3+-doped narsarsukite obtained by the sol-gel method still contained very small amounts of impurities that were only detected by photoluminescence spectroscopy due to the presence of europium cations. Although the term “doped” was used to refer to a Ln-containing material, the solid was prepared by adding europium nitrate pentahydrate to the sodium nitrate solution at the time of the synthesis.

Ferdov and co-workers [33,34] reported the synthesis of two different europiumdoped microporous titanosilicates, one analogue of the mineral sitinakite and the other analogue of the mineral ivanyukite. Curiously, when the latter titanosilicate was synthesized [34], its mineral analogue had not yet been discovered, and thus the authors referred to it as an analogue of pharmacosiderite (a hydrated arsenate mineral) due to their structural similarities. In 2009, Yakovenchuk et al., [80] reported the existence of the mineral ivanyukite, a titanosilicate of the pharmacosiderite type whose distinct nomenclature was given due to observable differences on the symmetry of the crystal structure caused by the existence of an extraframework cation [80,81].

Concerning the doping of both materials with Eu3+, Ferdov et al., [33,34] did not follow the common procedure described previously for ETS-10 and synthetic umbite because the calcination was not necessary. Hence, after the synthesis, sitinakite and ivanyukite were doped with the lanthanide by means of a conventional ion exchange, creating new optical materials that display a stable room temperature emission in the red spectral region. Ferdov et al., [33,34] studied the properties and the distribution of Eu3+ local coordination sites within the framework on the basis of photoluminescence spectroscopic data. This information could only be disclosed by photoluminescence since Eu3+-doped sitinakite and Eu3+-doped ivanyukite retained their structural integrity and the inclusion of Eu3+ resulted in a considerable crystallinity reduction, precluding Xray diffraction analysis as characterization technique. The unit cell volume of the Eu3+- doped sitinakite is almost the double of its native Na-form, suggesting a different distribution of the lanthanide cations within the pore system. A similar effect was also observed in its H-form, as well as in the K+-, Cs+- and Sr2+-exchanged forms of titanium and titano-niobium sitinakite. It is worth noting that the authors made chemical analyses by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and did not detect the presence of any sodium, which confirmed total exchange by europium. Considering that the substitution of Na+ by Eu3+ is not isovalent, one may expect a low occupancy of the cation sites in the structure of Eu3+-doped sitinakite.

Based on crystallographic data, Ferdov et al., [33] also suggested that Eu3+- and K+-exchanged sitinakites exhibit the same space group, and that both cations should have similar positions. Furthermore, they reasonably assume that the coordination configuration of Eu3+ is similar to that of K+. Taking into account it is impossible to determine the exact crystallographic positions of the europium cations, Ferdov et al., indicated that the estimated structural similarity between both exchanged materials suggests that to some extent Eu3+ inherit the positions of K+. In fact the photoluminescence study indicated the presence of two active europium sites, which supported crystallographic investigations, although possible surface-bonded Eu3+ could not be excluded. The presence of two distinct europium environments in Eu3+-doped ivanyukite was also noticed. The detailed emission spectra of Eu3+-doped sitinakite and Eu3+-doped ivanyukite recorded at 14 K and excited at 393 and 280 nm, respectively, are shown in Figure 7. The spectra display the typical Eu3+ orange-red intra-4f6 lines attributed to the 5D 7F transitions. For Eu3+-doped sitinakite, two peaks are unequivocally discerned for the 5D 7F transition (Figure 7.b), and the Stark field splitting of the 5D07F1 and 5D07F2 transitions are 4 and 6 clearly expressed components. Taking into account that the maximum splitting allowed for 5D 7F is 2j+1, only 1, 3 and 5 peaks were expected for a single site, which definitely indicates the presence of, at least, two different Eu3+ local environments in Eu3+-doped sitinakite (see Table 1). The 5D lifetimes at 14 K through the emission decay curves of two 5D07F0 are 0.501 ± 0.086 ms (Eu1) and 0.215 ± 0.013 ms (Eu2). Relatively to Eu3+- doped ivanyukite, the 14 K emission spectrum does not strongly evidence the presence of two local environments. Nevertheless, it contains a 5D07F1 transition displaying four expressed components (Figure 7.c) and a broad red-shifted 5D07F0 transition, which discloses the presence of two distinct Eu3+ environments (see Table 1). This last result seemed to be very strange since the exchangeable cations (Na+, K+ or Cs+) only occupy one crystallographic position, facing the cube centres of the structure. However, Ferdov et al., [33] explained that such behaviour was caused by the possibility of lattice distortion with the incorporation of europium ions, opening space for the creation of other europium environment.
## 2.2. Lanthanide silicates
## 2.2.1. Microporous lanthanide silicates
## Materials resembling montregianite

Montregianite is a very rare hydrous sodium potassium yttrium silicate (Na K Y Si O ·10H O) from Mont St. Hilaire, Quebéc, Canada, where it occurs in miarolitic cavities and as thermally metamorphosed inclusions and rheomorphic breccias in nepheline syenite [82,83]. In nature, this mineral usually occurs with substitution of some yttrium by cerium (CeO6 octahedra instead of YO6 octahedra).

Rocha and co-workers published the synthesis and structural characterization of microporous yttrium and calcium silicates, AV-1 (synthetic montregianite) and AV-2 [84,85], respectively, and the pure cerous montregianite AV-5, [36]. The crystal structure of montregianite and AV-1 consists of 8-membered rings double silicate sheets separated by octahedral sheets composed of YO and three non-equivalent NaO4(H2O)2 octahedra [85].

The first examples of microporous Eu(III) and Tb(III) silicates (Na4K2Ln2Si16O38·xH2O, Ln = Eu, Tb) in montregianite mineral group were reported by Ananias and co-workers and the materials are called AV-9 [37]. The main objective of their essay was to explore the possibility of combining, in a given silicate microporosity and optical activity. These researchers attributed to the Ln-materials a great potential for photonic applications, as light sources, X-ray phosphors, detector systems, and light-emitting diodes. Perhaps more important, they can be also used in magnetic resonance imaging, targeted radiotherapy, and as alternatives to radioimmune assay probes.

The structures of Ln-AV-9 and montregianite are related. Ln-AV-9 consists of two different types of layers alternating along the [100] direction as can be seen in Figure 8: (i) a double silicate sheet, where the single silicate sheet is of the apophylite type with 4- and 8-membered rings (Figure 8.a) and (ii) an open octahedral sheet, composed of two non-equivalent LnO6 octahedra and two distinct NaO4(H2O)2 octahedra (Figure 8.b). Within the large channels formed by the planar 8-membered silicate rings are located the ten-coordinated potassium cations (providing ion exchange capability) and the water molecules. The differences between Ln-AV-9 and montregianite are in the constitution of the octahedral (Na, Y, Eu and Tb) layers [37], being particularly important on the specific luminescence properties of AV-9. The former one contains two kinds of Eu(III) and Tb(III) sites, where one is isolated by NaO4(H2O)2 octahedra and the other faces the pores, while the latter contains a single kind of Y(III), facing the pores. Curiously, Ananias et al., [37] referred that photoluminescence studies on Eu-AV-9 disclosed the presence of two distinct Eu(III) local environments, corroborating the crystallographic structure previously described (Table 1). This is clearly disclosed in Figure 9 where the full width at half-maximum of its 5D07F0,2 transitions changed as the excitation wavelength varied from 394 (line a) to 527 nm (line c). The number of distinct 7F2-6 Stark components on the spectrum of Tb-AV-9, as well as their intensity variation with the excitation wavelength, do not allow the identification of more than one local metal site environment [37]. However, the authors affirmed that the presence of two distinct Tb(III) locals (Table 1) was clearly inferred by the analysis of the corresponding 5D4 decay curves (excited at 486 nm and detected at the strongest 5D47F5 transition line), which were well fitted by biexponential functions, yielding lifetimes of 3.50 ± 0.01 ms and 0.75 ± 0.01 ms. Later, the same researchers synthesized the first examples of siliceous materials combining zeolite-like properties with X-ray induced luminescence and infrared emission [86]. Also, Pereira and coworkers [87,88] published studies about NMR relaxivity of Ln-AV-9 because, due to the incorporation of the Ln3+ ions in the rigid framework (making their leaching virtually impossible), they have potential applications in combined therapy and imaging.

Zanardi et al., [38] synthesized, characterized and studied the thermal behaviour (at Eni laboratories) of a novel microporous gadolinium silicate, Na8K4Gd4Si32O76·17H2O, named EMS-6 (Eni MetalloSilicate number 6). Its crystal structure is very similar to the other members of the montregianite family, but careful inspection shows some differences on the coordination number of some elements. For instance, the Na+ cation is six-coordinated in montregianite but 7-coodinated in EMS-6: five framework oxygen atoms and two water molecules. The channel system of EMS-6 offers four extra-framework positions, one attributed to potassium and the others to water molecules. Ghose et al., [83] reported that the potassium site in montregianite is split in two non-equivalent positions, but Zanardi et al., [38] were not able to detect this event (thought did not exclude it). As can be seen in Figure 10, only one potassium site with full occupancy in the channel of EMS-6 was 9-fold coordinated (one water molecule less than that in montregianite).

The crystallization temperature for EMS-6 is critical. At a molar Si/Gd ratio of 20, regardless of the crystallization time, pure EMS-6 phase has been obtained at 200 ºC while at 170 ºC a mixture of EMS-6 and Gd-AV-20 was observed [38]. Additionally, dehydration-rehydration experiments showed that EMS-6 was able to be rehydrated after heated up to 700 ºC in a thermobalance at heating rate of 10 ºC/min. Nonetheless, at higher temperature (800 ºC) the structure suffers reorganization and a new crystalline phase named EMS-6b became stable. Such feature, well-known in zeolites [89,90] and in some microporous OPT materials [91–93], involved both the octahedra and tetrahedra layers and is ascribable to the loss of water and consequent reorganization of the sodium and potassium cations. After dehydration, the EMS-6 and EMS-6b samples were exposed to ambient conditions but only EMS-6 was capable of rehydrate.

Recently, Munhá et al. [39] reported the synthesis and the structural characterization of two novel trivalent neodymium microporous silicates: KNa2Nd[Si8O19]·5H2O and KNa2Nd[Si8O19]·2.8H2O. The latter was obtained by mildly heating (200 ºC) the former, and the authors claimed that it is to date the lanthanidecontaining rhodesite (montregianite group) analogue with the lowest content of water molecules in its structure. Both solids possess a single crystallographic independent Nd3+ metal centre, which is in contrast with, for example, the AV-9 solids published by Ananias et al. [37] that have two distinct metal environments instead. They also have three different Si sites, seven O sites, two Na sites and one exchangeable K+ site. KNa2Nd[Si8O19]·5H2O possesses three water oxygen (OW) sites, while KNa2Nd[Si8O19]·2.8H2O contains only two OW due to fully elimination of O3W site upon dehydration. Munhá et al. [39] concluded that the NdO octahedral environments present in both solids are significantly more regular than those observed for AV-9 materials. A special feature of these compounds is the fact that the layer composed by NaO6 parallel to the b plane is composed of partially occupied cations (50%), meaning that half of the sites are lacunae randomly distributed.
## Materials resembling tobermorite

Until the work of Ferreira et al., [23] the synthesis of novel microporous Ln-silicates by embedding stoichiometric amounts of Ln3+ cations on the microporous framework was carried out only in two systems: the synthetic analogues of mineral montregianite [36,37] and in an open framework cerium silicate, Na4.8Ce2Si12O30·4H2O [22]. Ferreira et al., [23] reported the synthesis and characterization of Ln-silicates denoted by AV-20 (Na K Ln Si O ·1.78H O, Ln = Gd, Eu, Tb, Sm, Ce) whose structures resemble tobermorites, a group of calcium silicate minerals used in cement hydration and as cation exchangers [94]. In tobermorite structure the silicate chains are of the wollastonite type and run along the [110] direction, on both sides of the Ln3+/Na+ containing layers. These chains are built up of Si2O7 units (paired Si1 and Si3 centred tetrahedron), which are linked through a bridging (Si2 centred) tetrahedron. Two wollastonite-type chains lying on the symmetry plane normal to [001] are condensed through the bridging oxygen O5, forming a double silicate chain and originating an 8- membered ring (see Figure 11.a). Each siliceous chain connects to a column of calcium polyhedra by Si2O7 sharing the oxygens of the capping ligands, as can be seen in Figure 11.b. The bridging tetrahedron shares the capping O6 ligand of the neighbouring columns. Tobermorites 11 Å are known as “anomalous” or “normal”, respectively, depending on whether they transform or not into tobermorites 9 Å upon calcination at ca. 300ºC [23,95]. Furthermore, the “anomalous” one contains only zeolitic water molecules while in “normal” tobermorites there are also Ca2+ cations inside the cavities.

The structure of Eu-AV-20 resembles tobermorite since the substitution of two Ca2+ by one Eu3+ and one Na+ occurs being also seven-coordinated. Some europium cations (ca. 10%) are disordered over the sodium sites, and thus columns of Eu/Na polyhedra running along [110] direction and neighbouring in each layer exist in the AV-20 form. These columns possess enough structural flexibility for hosting at least two different ions, like Eu3+ and Tb3+ or Gd3+ and Tb3+ [23]. Similarly to the mineral, the synthetic material has the Eu/Na polyhedral layers connected through the double silicate chains (wollastonite) building up a framework with channels running along [110] direction. These channels can be accessed through the double silicate chains of 8- membered rings and contain Na+ and K+ ions. The Na+ is six-coordinated to three framework oxygen atoms and three water molecules, while the K+ is seven-coordinated to four framework oxygen atoms and three water molecules. Both sites (particularly the sodium site) may be partially occupied by water molecules. Eu-AV-20 does not have “anomalous” or “normal” forms since even containing large amounts of cations in the cavities its structure is not transformed by calcination up to 800ºC [23].

With respect to photoluminescence studies, Ferreira et al., [23] reported the room temperature emission spectra shown in Figure 12. The typical 5D07F0−4 transitions are presented and the Stark field splitting of the 5D07F1,2 transitions are 4 and 6 clearly expressed components, respectively. Furthermore, two peaks are unequivocally discerned for the 5D07F0 transition (inset of Figure 12), revealing the existence of two europium sites (Table 1), one corresponds to Eu3+ in regular positions (Eu1) and another probably associated to the europium ions that are disordered over the Na+ sites (Eu2). The emission spectra also exposed the intensity ratio of 60% of Eu1 and 40% of Eu2, being different to the 90:10 proportion from the structural analysis. This phenomenon can be due to different absorption cross-sections and/or the possible occurrence of distinct nonradiative deactivations. The 5D0 decay curves detected in the 5D07F0 region at two distinct wavelengths associated to Eu1 and Eu2 can be well fitted by single exponential functions, yielding lifetimes 1.68 ± 0.02 ms (Eu1) and 1.66 ± 0.02 ms (Eu2).

The structure of Ln-AV-20 allows the introduction of a mixture of lanthanide ions into the framework without changing the crystal structure. In fact, Evans and coworkers [96,97] studied the possibility of tuning the emission colour in mixed Ln-AV-20 through energy transfer between the Ln-sites, its composition and chromaticity. The authors reported the preparation of Ln-AV-20 containing two (Ln = Gd1-aTba or Tb1- aEua) [96] and three different Ln3+ ions (Ln = Gd1-a-bTbaEub or Ce1-a-bTbaEub) [97]. The ionic radius of all lanthanide cations are comparable and therefore they should not significantly change the interatomic distances within the AV-20 layers.

Regarding the material with Gd Tb Eu and considering that Gd3+ does not emit in the visible while Tb3+ and Eu3+ emit in the green and red spectral regions, respectively, the authors reported that on excitation into Gd3+, as three energy transfer modes are available (Gd3+Tb3+, Gd3+Eu3+, Tb3+Eu3+) the relative lanthanide composition is less important. The sample emits in the yellow region due to combined emission from terbium and europium [97]. Nonetheless, on excitation into Tb3+, the sample composition becomes more important because, in this case, the Gd3+ cations act as blocks to energy migration, reducing the efficiency of Tb3+Eu3+ energy transfer. Hence, modifying the sample composition, i.e. by changing the concentration of gadolinium “blocks”, it is possible to fine-tune the emission colour of these materials in the red-green spectral region. Furthermore, via substituting Gd3+ by Ce3+, Evans et al., prepared a full-colour phosphor [97]. The same were observed in the material with two lanthanide ions in the structure [96] since the presence of one lanthanide caused energy transfer to another, which allowed to tune the emission colour of the material. The photoluminescence studies indicated that the two kinds of lanthanide optical centres (for example in Eu/Tb-AV-20) are near each other, which means that there is no clustering of a lanthanide in a separate crystal domain.
## Materials resembling sazhinite

A detailed study of the structure and photoluminescence properties of a microporous lanthanide silicate with general formula Na Ln Si O ·xH O (Ln = La3+, Sm3+, Eu3+, Tb3+ and Gd3+), named AV-21, was reported by Kowalchuk et al., [98]. The work on AV-21 [40] showed that its structure and the structure of other materials [22,99,100] resemble sazhinite [98,101]. The orthorhombic crystal structure of Sm-AV-21 possesses two crystallographically independent silicon centres, Si1 and Si2, which are part of the basic building tetrahedra of a woollastonite-like silicate chain running parallel to the [100] direction. The structural distinction between the two silicon atoms arises primarily from the neighbouring sodium cation centres since while Na1 is integrated within the corrugated anionic layers, the Na2 is located within the structural cavities. Adjacent chains merge through an oxygen atom (O3), which leads to the formation of a corrugated chain composed of 5-membered Si rings. Further, these rippled chains are interconnected by another oxygen atom (O5) leading to 8-membered Si-rings and to the formation of the undulated anionic [Si O 2-] layer extended in the ac plane. The neighbouring anionic [Si2O52-]8 layers are interconnected along the [010] direction by SmO6 octahedra, forming a three-dimensional anionic framework (as can be seen in

Figure 13), which is similar to the mineral sazhinite [101]. A lanthanum mineral analogue [99], a cerium silicate [22], and the α- and β- forms of a neodymium silicate [100] presenting such similarity were also reported.

High-resolution single-crystal synchrotron X-ray diffraction analysis showed that the crystallographic position of Na1 is also disordered over Sm2 centre. Although this phenomenon seemed strange, Jeong and co-workers [22] had already assisted and reported an apparent discrepancy in the overall charge of a cerium analogue due to the appearance of an unknown ratio of Ce3+ and Ce4+ centres. Furthermore, Kowalchuk et al., [98] affirmed that from a pure geometrical perspective, the disorder is much facilitated by minimal framework strain due to size similarity between the cationic radius of Ln3+ and Na+. In this study, the excitation and emission spectra of Eu-AV-21 were used as reference to describe the crystal structure and the disordered nature of Sm-AV-21. The room temperature photoluminescent emission spectrum of Eu-AV-21 excited at 392 nm is represented in Figure 14. It does not provide direct evidence for the presence of two Eu3+ sites in AV-21 since only one peak is observed in the 5D 7F transition and they cannot be rationalized from the splitting of the 5D 7F states. The 5D0 decay curves detected within the 5D07F1 are well fitted by a single exponential function because the lifetimes of the two Eu3+ local sites (see Table 1) are very similar and not distinguishable, yielding the value 2.95 ± 0.01 ms or 3.68 ± 0.01 ms, for the hydrated and anhydrous materials, respectively. Moreover, in mixed Eu/Tb-AV-21 framework the emission spectra demonstrated Tb3+Eu3+ energy transfer mostly due to the Ln1-Ln2 short distance (about 3.8 Å), which offers an efficient route for energy migration between optical centres.

The use of La3+ ions in the synthesis gel leads to a different material (La-AV-21), composed of very thin plates whose structure is very similar to Na2.4CeSi6O15·2.6H2O, a material reported by Wang and co-workers [55]. The tetrahedral nodes are also interconnected into wollastonite-like silicate chains running parallel to the [100] direction as previously described to Sm-AV-21, though the coalescence of neighbouring chains is different leading to a distinct [Si6O156-]8 layer. Half of the chains are joined together as in the Sm-AV-21 causing the corrugated chains composed of alternating 5-membered Si rings, while the other half coalesce in such a way that a chain composed of alternating 4- and 6-membered rings are formed instead. The authors [98] emphasized that such decrease on symmetry of [Si6O156-]8 layers was accompanied by a duplication of the corresponding unit cell axis. The La-AV-21 material contains a single crystallographic independent La3+ centre that exhibits a LaO7 coordination sphere identical to a highly distorted trigonal prism. The same as in Sm-AV-21 material, the adjacent anionic [Si6O156-]8 layers are interconnected by the La1

centres in the [010] direction, which leads to a porous 3-dimensional anionic framework having two types of 8-membered ring channels that contain the charge-balancing sodium cations and three crystallographic independent water molecules.

Microporous sodium cerium silicate Na CeSi O ·2.6H O containing mixed valence Ce(III)/Ce(IV) was successfully synthesized under mild hydrothermal conditions by Wang and co-workers [55] and examined for its ion exchange capacity. Additionally, the authors also inspected the ability to control the Ce(III)/Ce(IV) ratio present by framework oxidation/reduction. Also, Jeong et al., [22] studied the ability to tune the sorption capacity as well as the photoluminescence properties of this Ce(III)/Ce(IV)-containing material with the structure similar to Sm-AV-21. Both authors suggested that when Ce(IV) content increased, less extra-framework cations were required to balance the charge of the anionic framework, and thus changed its sorption characteristics. The framework connectivity of this material published by Wang et al [55] is similar to that reported for La-AV-21, whose difference lies on the charge of the required compensation cations. Since less cations are required by Ce(III)/Ce(IV)- containing materials, a redistribution of cations and water molecules inside the pores and channels occurs and thus, the Na+ site in 8-membered ring channels has only an occupancy of 70% while the site in 6-membered ring channels is fully occupied. The presence of Na+ in the open channels implies a high ion mobility. In fact, ion exchange experiments proved that the sodium cations located in the channels could be exchanged by others, such as NH +, Li+, K+, Ag+, Pb2+, Mg2+, Ca2+ and Ba2+ under microwave radiation. The ion exchange selectivity sequence obtained by Wang et al., [55] was: NH4+ (97.2%) > Ag+ (63.2%) > Li+ (50.0%) > K+ (35.8%) > Mg2+ (21.7%) > Ca2+ (8.6%) > Pb2+ (7.9%) > Ba2+ (0.9%). Moreover, the Na+ ions are almost completely exchanged by NH4+.

The various silicates previously reported [22,36,55,102] contain cerium atoms with different valence states (some are Ce3+-containing silicates and others Ce3+/Ce4+ mixed ones). Following this line of though, Wang and co-workers [56] published the first examples of Ce4+ and Ce4+/Ti4+ mixed silicates synthesized under mild hydrothermal conditions at 503 K, Na8CeSi6O18 and Na8Ce0.73Ti0.27Si6O18, respectively. The authors describe the single-crystal structure of the Na8CeSi6O18 material as constructed from the [Si6O18]n12n- cyclosilicate ring anions linked via CeO6 octahedra. UV-Vis absorption spectroscopy gives a broad band that is characteristic of octahedrally coordinated titanium, which means that Ti atoms may partially substitute the octahedral Ce sites in the Na8Ce0.73Ti0.27Si6O18 material. In this seminal material, each asymmetric unit contains one crystallographically independent Ce atom, one distinct Si atom, and three distinct Na atoms. Ce atom is six-coordinated to oxygen atoms to form an octahedron, while each Si atom is four-coordinated to oxygen atoms to form a tetrahedron. The CeO6 and the SiO4 link each other by the oxygen vertex to form a three-dimensional framework with 6-membered ring channels along the [101] direction. The sodium cations are responsible for achieving the charge-balance and thus, Na1 and Na2 are alternately arranged around the SiO tetrahedron of the 6- membered rings in the cyclosilicate anions viewed from the [001] direction, while Na3 cations reside in the centre of the 6-membered ring channels along the [101] direction.

The strong red emitter Na Eu Si O 3D framework published by Liu et al. [41] is also based on the [Si6O18]n12n- cyclosilicate ring anions connected via EuO6. The 6- membered ring channels along the [010] direction are delimited by six SiO tetrahedra that belong to one cyclosilicate, while the 8-membered rings channels along [110] direction are formed by eight SiO4 tetrahedra that belong to four different cyclosilicate anions. Each asymmetric unit contains one distinct Eu site, two symmetrically independent Si sites and four distinct Na sites. The charge balancing sodium cations are located in the 4- and 6-membered ring (Na1 and Na4) along the [010] direction and in the 6- and 8-membered rings channels (Na2 and Na3) along the [110] direction. Single-crystal X-ray analysis revealed that the crystallographic positions of Na2 and Na3 are shared with partially occupied Eu2 and Eu3 centres, respectively, which was confirmed by the photoluminescent studies.
## Materials resembling apatite

The last years were prolific on the synthesis of materials resembling the mineral apatite [59–61]. Apatite is a group of phosphate minerals that are hexagonal in symmetry with composition variations in the anion site. The nomenclature with the apatite mineral is extensive and overlapping but its formula is usually Ca10(PO4)6X2 (X = F, Cl, Br or OH). The general formulae of materials with apatite-type structure is AxLn10-x(BO4)XY where A = Ca, K or Na; B = P, Si or Ge; and X, Y = O or F.

Lanthanide silicates can possess apatite-type structure in special composition. Latshaw and co-workers [61] presented the crystal structures of seven new apatite oxides and oxyfluorides, along with the photoluminescence and magnetic properties of NaEu9(SiO4)6O2, Na1.5Eu8.5(SiO4)6OF, Eu9.34(SiO4)6O2 and Gd9.34(SiO4)6O2, synthesized via flux growth in selected alkali-fluoride melts. The crystallographic studies revealed that the structure embody two unique lanthanide polyhedra (Ln1 and Ln2) and isolated SiO tetrahedra and an O4 oxygen site that contains either O2-, F- or a mix of both. Ln1 is located at a six-coordinated twisted trigonal prism, while Ln2 is located at a sevencoordinated distorted pentagonal bipyramid. Ln1 and Ln2 form individually columns down the c-axis. The former are created by face-shared stacking of their distorted
